definition: Confederation is when several separate British colonies joined together in 1867 to form one country: Canada.
Canada's official name at Confederation in 1867 — "Dominion" was the term Canadians chose instead of calling the new country a kingdom or republic.
The politicians from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and the old Province of Canada who met in the 1860s and hammered out the deal that created Canada.
The 1867 law passed by the British Parliament that actually created Canada. It's still in force today, just renamed the Constitution Act, 1867.
Canada's founding constitutional law — the 1867 version created the country, and a 1982 version added the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and brought the constitution fully under Canadian control.

A system where the people running the government (the Cabinet) only stay in power as long as they have the support of the majority of elected representatives — not because a governor simply appointed them.
Colonists who stayed loyal to the British Crown during the American Revolution and fled to Canada afterward, settling mostly in what's now Ontario and the Maritimes.
A war between the United States and Britain (fought partly on Canadian soil) that ended in a stalemate — but it's remembered here because it kept Canada from being absorbed into the U.S.
A decree from King George III that first recognized Indigenous peoples' rights to their land — it's the starting point for the treaty relationship between the Crown and First Nations.
The Manitoba settlement where, in 1869-70, the Métis rose up under Louis Riel after Canada tried to take over the territory without consulting the people already living there.
A second uprising led by Louis Riel and the Métis, this time in Saskatchewan, that ended with Riel's trial and execution for treason.
Short for North West Mounted Police — the force created in 1873 to police the newly settled Canadian West. It later became the RCMP.
A period in the 1960s when Quebec rapidly modernized and moved away from Church control, and when Quebec nationalism (the idea of Quebec as a distinct society) grew stronger.
A 1969 federal law that made English and French equal languages across the federal government, guaranteeing Canadians the right to federal services in either one.
A First World War battle (1917) where Canadian troops fought together as one force for the first time and won — often called the moment Canada started feeling like a real nation.
The final string of Allied victories that ended the First World War in 1918, with Canadian troops under General Arthur Currie playing a leading role.
June 6, 1944 — the day Allied forces landed in Normandy, France, to begin liberating Europe from Nazi occupation. Canadian troops led one of the five landing beaches.
The stretch of Normandy coastline that Canadian soldiers were assigned to capture on D-Day in 1944.
The Second World War naval campaign where Canadian warships helped protect supply convoys crossing the Atlantic from German submarines.
Not an actual railroad — a secret network of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape the United States to freedom in Canada in the 1800s.
A fee the Canadian government charged Chinese immigrants (and only Chinese immigrants) to enter the country, starting in the 1880s. Canada formally apologized for it in 2006.
A rush of prospectors into the Yukon in the 1890s after gold was discovered in the Klondike region, quickly turning a remote territory into a boomtown.
A system of government where a king or queen is the official head of state, but real day-to-day power rests with an elected government acting within the rules of a constitution.
Canada's head of state — currently King Charles III. The role is symbolic and non-partisan; the elected Prime Minister and Cabinet actually run the country.

Another name for the Sovereign's role as head of state — used to talk about the authority of the monarchy as an institution, separate from whoever happens to be king or queen at the time. You'll see it in phrases like "Crown land" (government-owned land) or "the Crown prosecutes" (the government brings criminal charges, not a private citizen).

The Sovereign's representative in Canada, appointed on the Prime Minister's advice. The Governor General performs ceremonial duties and formally signs bills into law, but doesn't make political decisions.
The Sovereign's representative in each province — basically the provincial version of the Governor General.

The federal government's representative in each of Canada's three territories (Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut) — similar to a Lieutenant Governor, but appointed by Ottawa rather than the Sovereign.
A vote in the House of Commons on a major issue (like the budget) that tests whether the governing party still has enough support to keep governing. Losing one usually triggers an election.
When the House of Commons votes against the government on a major issue, showing it no longer has majority support — this can force the government to resign or call an election.
Canada's federal law-making body, made up of three parts working together: the Sovereign (represented by the Governor General), the Senate, and the House of Commons.
The elected chamber of Parliament, where Members of Parliament (MPs) debate and vote on laws. This is the chamber that actually decides who forms the government.
Parliament's second chamber, whose members (Senators) are appointed rather than elected. It reviews and can propose changes to bills passed by the House of Commons.
A member of the Senate, appointed by the Governor General on the Prime Minister's advice, who serves until age 75.
The final formal step that turns a bill into law — the Governor General signs it on the Sovereign's behalf, after it has already passed both the House of Commons and the Senate.
Another word for an electoral district — the specific geographic area whose voters elect one Member of Parliament (or one provincial representative).
The Prime Minister and the ministers chosen to run government departments (like Health or Finance). Cabinet proposes most new laws and the federal budget.
The opposition party with the most seats in the House of Commons — its job is to challenge and hold the government to account.
A government where the winning party holds more than half the seats in the House of Commons, letting it pass laws without needing support from other parties.
A government where the winning party holds less than half the seats in the House of Commons, meaning it needs support from at least one other party to pass laws.

A system of government where power is divided between a national (federal) government and provincial/territorial governments, each with its own areas of responsibility — e.g. Ottawa handles national defence and citizenship, while provinces run health care and education.
The head of a provincial or territorial government — the provincial equivalent of the Prime Minister.
Member of the Legislative Assembly — what an elected provincial representative is called in most provinces and territories.
Member of the National Assembly — what an elected provincial representative is called in Quebec.
Member of Provincial Parliament — what an elected provincial representative is called in Ontario.
Member of the House of Assembly — what an elected provincial representative is called in Newfoundland and Labrador.
The independent federal agency responsible for running elections and keeping the national list of registered voters.
A local law passed by a municipal (city or town) council, covering things like parking, noise, or property standards.
The elected leadership of a First Nation, made up of a chief and councillors, responsible for local services like housing, schools, and roads on the reserve.
The principle that everyone — including the government itself — has to follow the law. No one is above it.
The principle that the government must follow fair, established legal procedures before it can take away someone's rights, freedom, or property.
The rule that anyone accused of a crime is treated as innocent unless and until a court actually proves them guilty.
An old legal right letting someone who's been detained by the state demand to be brought before a court, so a judge can decide whether the detention is actually lawful.
Canada's highest court — its decisions are final, and every other court in the country has to follow them.
The court that handles legal cases specifically involving the federal government, such as immigration or federal agency decisions.
The name used in some provinces (instead of "Superior Court") for the main trial-level court that hears serious criminal and civil cases.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police — Canada's national police force, which also acts as the provincial police in most provinces (all except Ontario and Quebec).
A famous RCMP ceremonial performance where uniformed Mounties on horseback perform intricate formations — a well-known symbol of the force.
Part of Canada's constitution (added in 1982) that guarantees Canadians' basic rights and freedoms — like freedom of speech, equality rights, and the right to a fair trial.
The Charter's four basic freedoms guaranteed to everyone in Canada: freedom of conscience and religion, freedom of thought and expression, freedom of peaceful assembly, and freedom of association.
The Charter right letting Canadian citizens live, work, and travel freely anywhere in Canada.
Canada's official heraldic symbol — a shield-and-crest design combining English, French, Scottish, and Irish emblems along with maple leaves, used on official documents and buildings.
Canada's national motto, Latin for "from sea to sea" — it appears on the coat of arms.
The flag Canada used for about 100 years before the current maple leaf flag was adopted in 1965 — it had the Union Jack in the corner and Canada's coat of arms.
A stylized lily symbol tied to French royal history — it's the central image on Quebec's flag.
Canada's own national honour, created in 1967, given to people who've made an outstanding contribution to the country.
The highest award for bravery available to Canadian and Commonwealth armed forces members.
A ceremonial gold staff carried into the House of Commons before each sitting — it represents the authority of Parliament, and no formal business can happen without it present.
The tall clock tower on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, built as a memorial to Canadians who died in the First World War.
Books kept inside the Peace Tower that record the names of every Canadian who has died in military service.
The championship trophy of the National Hockey League, originally donated by a Governor General of Canada in 1892.
The championship trophy of the Canadian Football League, originally donated by a Governor General of Canada in 1909.
Canada's military air-show flight team, officially 431 Air Demonstration Squadron, known for their precision flying formations.
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade — a post-Second World War treaty that lowered trade barriers between countries. It eventually evolved into the World Trade Organization.
The World Trade Organization — the international body that sets and enforces the rules of global trade between countries, including Canada.
The North American Free Trade Agreement — a 1994 deal that removed most trade barriers between Canada, the United States, and Mexico.
A group of the world's major industrialized economies (including Canada) whose leaders meet regularly to coordinate on global economic issues.
The federal law that sets the rules every province's health care system has to follow in order to receive federal health funding.
Government pension programs (Quebec runs its own, separate from the rest of Canada) that workers pay into during their careers and draw retirement income from afterward, started in 1965.
A monthly government pension paid to most Canadians 65 and older, funded from general tax revenue rather than from contributions workers made during their careers.
A government program that provides temporary income support to workers who lose their job, funded by contributions from workers and employers.
A huge region of ancient, rocky terrain covering much of central and northern Canada — it's rich in minerals and forests but has poor farming soil.
The bridge connecting Prince Edward Island to mainland New Brunswick — at about 12.9 km, one of the longest bridges in the world over ice-covered water.
A bay between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick famous for having the highest tides in the world.
French colonists who settled the Maritime provinces starting in 1604 — many were forcibly deported by the British in the 1750s, an event known as the Great Upheaval.
Someone whose first or main language is English.
Someone whose first or main language is French.
A distinct Indigenous people descended from historical unions between First Nations and European (mostly French) settlers, with their own culture and language.
The traditional language of the Inuit, and one of the official languages of Nunavut.
A term for the Indigenous peoples of Canada who are not Inuit or Métis — there are over 600 First Nations across the country, each with its own culture and history.
Land set aside by the federal government specifically for the use of a First Nation.
Canada's youngest and northernmost territory, created in 1999, with a mostly Inuit population. The name means "our land" in Inuktitut.
North America's second-longest river system, flowing through the Northwest Territories to the Arctic Ocean.
A part-time reserve unit of the Canadian Armed Forces made up mostly of Indigenous and local volunteers, who patrol and watch over Canada's remote northern regions.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization — a military alliance of Canada, the U.S., and mostly-European countries, formed after the Second World War, where an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
The North American Aerospace Defence Command — a joint Canada-U.S. military command that watches North American airspace for threats.
An international organization of French-speaking countries and governments, which Canada helped found in 1970.
A voluntary association of mostly former British colonies, including Canada, that grew out of the British Empire. The Sovereign serves as its ceremonial head.
A robotic arm designed and built in Canada that was used on NASA's Space Shuttle to move cargo and help with repairs in orbit.

France's North American colony, founded in the early 1600s and centred on the St. Lawrence River in what's now Quebec. At its peak it stretched from Hudson Bay down to the Gulf of Mexico, but Britain took it over after defeating France at the Plains of Abraham in 1759.

The term Canada's citizenship material and Charter of Rights use for the country's original inhabitants as a group — First Nations, Inuit, and Métis together. They're one of Canada's three "founding peoples," alongside the French and the British; "Indigenous" is the more commonly used word today, but "Aboriginal" remains the official legal wording.

The name French-speaking Catholic settlers of New France called themselves (also "Habitants"). After Britain took over the colony in 1763, the Quebec Act of 1774 let them keep their Catholic faith, French civil law, and way of life.

A British fur-trading company chartered in 1670 and given exclusive trading rights over the huge Hudson Bay watershed (Rupert's Land). It dominated Canada's early fur trade for two centuries before selling its territory to the new Canadian government in 1869.

The vast territory draining into Hudson Bay — covering most of today's Prairies, northern Ontario and Quebec, and part of the Arctic — that Britain granted to the Hudson's Bay Company in 1670. Canada bought it in 1869, and it later became the base for Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut.
A Hudson's Bay Company fort at the meeting point of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, seized by Louis Riel and the Métis in the 1869-70 Red River uprising. It later grew into the city of Winnipeg.

French-Canadian canoemen hired by fur-trading companies to paddle trade goods and furs along the rivers and lakes of the fur-trade routes, often forming close alliances with First Nations along the way.

French for "runners of the woods" — independent, unlicensed fur traders (unlike the company-employed voyageurs) who lived and traded directly with First Nations deep in the woods, without a fur company's permission.

Government-funded, church-run boarding schools that operated from the 1800s to 1996, where Aboriginal children were often forcibly separated from their families with the goal of assimilating them into non-Indigenous culture. Conditions were frequently poorly funded and abusive, and the federal government formally apologized in 2008.

Short for the Canadian Pacific Railway — the transcontinental railway completed in 1885, financed by British and American investors and built largely by European and Chinese labourers, that physically linked Canada from coast to coast and is often called a symbol of the country's unity.
